lead: Over a long sight the Earth curves under the line of sight and air bends the sight downward. The curve makes the far staff read high; refraction makes it read slightly low. Curvature wins, so the net correction is subtracted. The combined correction enters every levelling specification that allows long sights. It matters at river crossings and valley sightings, where a millimetre decides a benchmark.
prereq: You need differential levelling and backsight–foresight booking from 3.3 and 3.4.

sections.h3: Curvature, refraction and a combined correction

blocks.text: Two staff stations A and B lie on the same level surface, a distance d apart, so the curvature effect is the same at either end. A horizontal sight from A runs straight; the curved ground falls below it. The staff at B stands on the curved ground, so a horizontal sight meets the staff higher than a true level line would. That gap is curvature correction C<sub>c</sub>. Pure geometry gives C<sub>c</sub> = d²/(2R), with d in metres and R ≈ 6 370 000 m. Convert d to km and use R = 6370 km to get the shortcut constant.
C<sub>c</sub> = 0.0785 d²,   C<sub>r</sub> = 0.0112 d²,   C = 0.0673 d²
blocks.where: d is sight length in km; C<sub>c</sub>, C<sub>r</sub> and C are curvature, refraction and combined corrections in metres.

blocks.text: Refraction bends the ray toward the ground by about one-seventh of the curvature, so it removes 0.0112 d². The net is C = 0.0673 d². Subtract C from every long-sight staff reading; the corrected reading is smaller. At 1 km C = 0.067 m; at 2 km C = 0.269 m.
Long sights over water cannot be balanced. Reciprocal levelling uses two setups, one near each staff, and swaps long and short sights.

items: Set the level close to A. Take the near reading r<sub>A</sub> on A, then the far reading r<sub>B</sub> on B.
Move the level close to B. Take the near reading r′<sub>B</sub> on B, then the far reading r′<sub>A</sub> on A.
Compute the true height difference and the residual error.

blocks.text: The near readings have almost no curvature, refraction or collimation error. Each far reading carries nearly the same error. The true height difference A minus B is h = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) + (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)]. Positive h means A is higher.

blocks.where: h is true height difference A minus B in metres; r<sub>A</sub>, r<sub>B</sub> are readings with the level near A; r′<sub>A</sub>, r′<sub>B</sub> are readings with the level near B.

blocks.text: The residual in one far sight is ε = ½[(r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub>) − (r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub>)]. ε should come out close to 0.0673 d², with d the long sight in km; any excess above that value is the collimation error of the instrument. Keep staffs vertical on firm ground.

figure.caption: Curvature rises as 0.0785 d²; the combined correction is lower because refraction opposes it. At 2 km the values are 0.314 m and 0.269 m.

spec.aria: Two rising curves against sight length: curvature reaches 0.314 metres at 2 kilometres and the combined curvature plus refraction correction reaches 0.269 metres.

examples.question: A river is about 1.2 km wide. With the level near A, the reading on A is 1.500 m and on B is 2.900 m. With the level near B, the reading on B is 2.800 m and on A is 1.600 m. Find the true height difference and the residual error in one far sight. Check against the combined curvature and refraction correction.
steps: First apparent difference = r<sub>B</sub> − r<sub>A</sub> = 2.900 − 1.500 = 1.400 m.
Second apparent difference = r′<sub>B</sub> − r′<sub>A</sub> = 2.800 − 1.600 = 1.200 m.
True difference h = ½(1.400 + 1.200) = 1.300 m. Positive, so A is higher than B.
Residual in one far sight ε = ½(1.400 − 1.200) = 0.100 m.
Combined correction for d = 1.2 km: C = 0.0673 × 1.2² = 0.0673 × 1.44 = 0.097 m.
The 0.100 m residual is close to 0.097 m; the 0.003 m remainder is the small collimation error.
examples.answer: The true difference is 1.300 m, A higher than B, with a 0.100 m residual in one far sight; the formula gives 0.097 m for 1.2 km.
examples.check:
d = 1.2
rA = 1.500
rB = 2.900
rA2 = 1.600
rB2 = 2.800
first = rB - rA
second = rB2 - rA2
h = (first + second) / 2
err = (first - second) / 2
formula = 0.0673 * d * d
print(round(first, 3))
print(round(second, 3))
print(round(h, 3))
print(round(err, 3))
print(round(formula, 3))

traps: Using metres in 0.0785 d². Convert first: a 200 m sight is d = 0.2 km, so C<sub>c</sub> = 0.0785 × 0.04 = 0.003 m, not 3140 m.
Adding the combined correction. Curvature makes the far staff read high, so subtract C from the staff reading.
Using 0.0785 d² as the combined correction. That is curvature only; refraction reduces it to 0.0673 d².
Reversing the reciprocal formula. Keep the same order: far minus near in each setup, then average.
Forgetting the residual half-difference. The averaged height is good, but the leftover estimates the far-sight error.

quiz.q: State the combined curvature and refraction correction formula and its units.
quiz.a: C = 0.0673 d² m, with d in km; subtract C from the staff reading.

quiz.q: Why is refraction smaller than curvature and opposite in sign?
quiz.a: Refraction bends the ray downward and reduces the staff reading by about one-seventh of curvature; net correction is curvature minus refraction.

quiz.q: A sight is 800 m long. Find the combined correction.
Reciprocal readings: near A, r<sub>A</sub> = 1.200 m and r<sub>B</sub> = 2.000 m; near B, r′<sub>A</sub> = 1.350 m and r′<sub>B</sub> = 1.950 m. Find h.
quiz.a: First = 0.800 m, second = 0.600 m, h = 0.700 m; A is higher than B.

quiz.q: For the previous question, find the residual and say what it suggests.
quiz.a: ε = ½(0.800 − 0.600) = 0.100 m. A large residual suggests collimation error or a setup change; compare with 0.0673 d² if d is known.

quiz.q: Why place the level near A and then near B?
quiz.a: The near reading is almost free of long-sight errors; each far sight gets similar error, and averaging cancels most of it.

quiz.q: Why not just apply the correction formula to both staff readings over water?
quiz.a: The formula needs sight length and assumes a steady atmosphere; over water, refraction and collimation vary. Reciprocal levelling measures the residual directly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Long-sight corrections reappear in dam crest monitoring, bridge-deck levelling, railway gradient checks and automated total-station networks. Modern instruments log temperature and pressure, but the geometry of curvature remains. Search terms: reciprocal levelling, curvature correction 0.0785, refraction coefficient, collimation error. Trigonometric heighting is Unit 4; the physics of atmospheric refraction is Unit 6.
